1.open: What is something you have made with your own hands that you were proud of, even a little?
questions: Verse 2 says the earth was "formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep." Why might the Bible begin with a picture of emptiness and darkness before God does anything?
Again and again we read "God said" and "it was so" (v. 3, v. 7). What does it tell us about God that he creates simply by speaking?
Seven times the chapter says God saw that something was good, for example "And God saw that it was good" (v. 10). What do you notice about the world that you would call good?

The sun and moon are only called "the greater light" and "the lesser light" (v. 16). Many scholars think this was a quiet way of saying they are made things, not gods. What do people today look to as if it were God, and how does this chapter speak to that?
Verse 27 says, "So God created man in His own image." What do you think it means to be made in God's image, and how would it change the way we treat people we find difficult?

In verse 28 God tells people to "subdue" the earth and "rule" over the animals. Some have read that as freedom to use nature as we like, and others as a duty to care for what still belongs to God. How do you hear it?
Verse 31 says God looked at all He had made and "it was very good." Where does that ring true in your experience, and where does it feel hard to believe? Say as much or as little as you like.

Christians read the six days in different ways: as ordinary days, as long ages, or as a patterned picture of who made the world and why. How can we hold our own view and still listen well to someone who sees it differently?
1.life: Once a day this week, stop for a minute and look closely at something God made, like a tree, the sky, or a person you love. Say a quiet thank you, and notice what you would call good about it.
1.prayer: Thank God for making the world and for calling it good. Ask Him to help you see other people as made in His image, and to care for the part of creation that is in your hands.
1.tip: The question of how to read the six days can swallow the whole evening. Say once, kindly, that Christians who love the Bible read it differently, then steer back to what everyone agrees on: God made everything, it is good, and people bear His image. Offer to talk more after the meeting.

2.open: What is a place you have been that felt peaceful, and what made it that way?
questions: Verse 3 says God "blessed the seventh day and sanctified it." What does it look like for you to stop and rest, and what gets in the way?
Verse 7 says God "formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils." What does it tell you about people that we are made of both dust and God's breath?
In verse 15 God places the man in the garden "to cultivate and keep it." Work comes before anything goes wrong. How does that fit or clash with how you think about your job or daily tasks?
God says, "You may eat freely from every tree of the garden," and then names one exception (v. 16). Why might it matter that the generous part comes first?

Verse 17 warns that eating from the one tree means "you will surely die." Readers understand this in different ways, such as becoming mortal, losing closeness with God, or both. What do you take from it, and what questions does it leave you with?
God says, "It is not good for the man to be alone" (v. 18). When have you felt that most sharply, and what eased it, if anything did?
Even with a garden and the animals, "no suitable helper was found" (v. 20). What does this suggest about what people need from one another that other good things cannot give?
Verse 25 says the man and his wife "were not ashamed." What would it be like to be fully known and still feel safe? Where do you long for that, or find it hard to believe?
2.life: Pick one stretch of time this week, even an hour, to stop work and rest on purpose. Then reach out to one person who may be feeling alone, with a call, a text or an invitation.
2.prayer: Thank God for the breath of life and for the people he has given you. Ask him to help you rest, to work well, and to notice someone who is alone.
2.tip: Verses 18 to 24 raise questions about men and women, and Christians read them differently: some see distinct roles, others a partnership of equals. Name that in one line, then steer back to what the text says about not being alone. Also be gentle with anyone who is single, widowed or lonely, since this chapter can sting. Make room for them to speak, and do not hurry to fix it.

3.open: When you were a kid, what is something you tried to hide from your parents, and how well did it work?
questions: The serpent starts with a question: "Did God really say, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden?'" (v. 1). How does it twist what God actually said, and where do you hear that kind of twisting today?
The serpent hints that God is holding something back: "you will be like God, knowing good and evil" (v. 5). Why is the idea that God is withholding something good so tempting to believe?

Verse 6 says the fruit was "good for food and pleasing to the eyes" and "desirable for obtaining wisdom." What does the woman see that makes it appealing, and how do similar pulls show up in your own life?
After they eat, they "knew that they were naked" and hid (vv. 7-8). They expected power and got shame. When have you wanted something and felt shame once you had it?
God asks, "Where are you?" (v. 9). Why might God ask a question He already knows the answer to, and what does it tell you about how God comes to people who have failed?
The man says, "The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit" and she says, "The serpent deceived me" (vv. 12-13). Blaming is easy. What makes it so hard to simply own up and say what you did?

God makes "garments of skin" and clothes them (v. 21), even as He sends them out. What does that small act show you about God? If you are unsure what you think of God in this chapter, what questions does it raise for you?

Christians read verse 15 and the word "seed" in different ways, and traditions explain how this chapter affects every person differently. How can your group hold those differences kindly while still talking about what the chapter shows about us?
3.life: This week, when you catch yourself explaining away a mistake or pointing at someone else, stop and say it plainly to God, and to the person involved if it fits. Use simple words that own what you did. Notice how it feels.
3.prayer: Thank God that He still comes looking for us, asking "Where are you?" Ask for honesty about where you hide or blame, and for trust that He is good.
3.tip: Questions about original sin, the serpent as Satan, and verses 15 and 16 can take over the evening. Say once that Christians disagree on these, briefly name that, and steer back to the story: the temptation, the hiding, the blaming, and God's care. Invite anyone with deeper questions to keep talking afterwards.

4.open: Did you grow up with brothers, sisters or close cousins? What is one thing you used to compete over?
questions: Verse 4 says Abel brought "the best portions of the firstborn of his flock," and verse 5 says God "had no regard for Cain and his offering." The text never says exactly why. What do you notice in these verses, and what do you wonder about?
Christians have given different reasons for God's response: Abel gave his best, Abel had real faith, or the text simply leaves it unexplained. Which of these makes the most sense to you, and why?
Verse 5 says Cain "became very angry, and his countenance fell." When you feel passed over or unfairly treated, what does that anger tend to look like in you?

God speaks to Cain before anything happens and says, "sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it" (v. 7). What do you make of God giving a warning and a way out? What might "crouching" look like in everyday life?
When God asks where Abel is, Cain answers, "Am I my brother's keeper?" (v. 9). Why do you think Cain answered that way, and how do we dodge responsibility for people today?
Cain says, "My punishment is greater than I can bear" (v. 13), yet God still places a mark on him so no one would kill him (v. 15). What does this show you about God, even in the middle of judgment?
Lamech boasts that if Cain is avenged sevenfold, "then Lamech seventy-sevenfold" (v. 24). How does this show where Cain's line is heading, and where do you see that same pride in revenge today?

The chapter ends with a new son and the line, "At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD" (v. 26). After so much loss, what does it mean to you that people kept turning to God? If that feels hard to say right now, what honestly gets in the way?
4.life: Think of one person you have felt jealous of or have kept at a distance. This week, do one small thing for their good: send a message, pray for them by name, or say something kind. If anger toward someone is crouching at your door, tell God about it plainly.
4.prayer: Thank God that he speaks to us before we go wrong and does not leave us alone with our anger. Ask for help to master what crouches at the door, and to care for the people he has put near you.
4.tip: Someone will want to settle why God rejected Cain's offering, and the text does not say. Name the different views briefly and kindly, then move the group to verses 6 and 7, where God's invitation to Cain is clear. Also be gentle with anyone carrying a painful family rift, and do not press people to share more than they want to.

5.open: Who in your family is the one who keeps track of the family history, and what is the best story they tell?
questions: The list begins by saying God made humans "in His own likeness" (v. 1). What difference does it make to say that every person carries God's likeness, including people we find hard to like?
Verse 3 says Adam "had a son in his own likeness, after his own image." What do you notice getting passed down in families, the good and the hard?
Verse after verse ends with the same words: "and then he died" (v. 5). Why do you think the writer repeats this so steadily? How does it land with you?

Many of these men lived over 900 years. Christians read those numbers in different ways, some as exact and some as a way of making a point. What do you take from the numbers, and what questions do they raise for you?

Of Enoch the text says, "Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away" (v. 24). What do you picture when you hear "walked with God"? What would that look like in an ordinary week?
Most people in this list are remembered by their years and their children. What do you think a short record like this would miss about a life? What would you want people to remember about yours?

Lamech names his son Noah and hopes he will "comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands" (v. 29). What are you hoping for relief from right now? If it is hard to hope for anything, you can say that too.

This chapter is a thread of ordinary families running toward Noah, and Christians also read it alongside Luke 3, which traces Jesus back to Adam. How does it change the way you see your own place in a long story?
5.life: Pick one older relative or friend this week and ask them about their life: where they grew up, what they worked at, what they learned. Listen for the things a list of dates would leave out.
5.prayer: Thank God that every person in every generation carries his likeness and is known by him. Ask to walk with him day by day, and pray for any family member who is on your heart.
5.tip: The ages in this chapter can swallow the whole evening. Say once, plainly, that Christians read the numbers differently, then steer back to the questions about God's likeness, death, Enoch and hope. Quiet members can answer question 7 honestly, so make clear that it is fine to say they are not sure they hope for much right now.

6.open: What is the biggest project you ever started that turned out to be much harder or longer than you expected?
questions: Verse 5 says "every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was altogether evil all the time." What do you think the writer wants us to see about the state of the world? How does it compare with what you see today?

Verses 1 to 4 are puzzling. Christians read the "sons of God" in different ways: heavenly beings, men from a faithful family line, or powerful rulers. Whichever reading you lean toward, what seems to be going wrong when they "took as wives whomever they chose" (v. 2)?
Verse 6 says the LORD "was grieved in His heart." What does it do to your picture of God to read that he feels sorrow over what people do?
Verse 11 says the earth was "full of violence," and God names that as the reason for the flood (v. 13). Where do you see violence, in big ways or small ones, that you wish God would deal with?
Verse 8 says "Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD," and verse 9 says he "walked with God." What do you think it looks like to walk with God while the people around you do not?
God tells Noah, "I will establish My covenant with you" (v. 18). Why might God make a promise to Noah before the flood even begins? What does that tell us about where this story is heading?

Verse 22 says Noah "did everything precisely as God had commanded him." Is there something you believe God has asked of you that feels big, slow or hard to understand? Or if you are not sure what God is asking, what is that like?
This is a hard chapter, and many people find the flood difficult to square with a loving God. What questions or discomfort does it raise for you? You do not need to have an answer.
6.life: Noah kept going in a world that did not share his faith. This week, pick one small, steady habit that keeps you close to God, such as a few minutes of reading or prayer each day, and keep it for seven days.
6.prayer: Thank God that he sees the pain and violence in the world and is not indifferent to it. Ask for the kind of trust that listens to him and follows through, as Noah did, and pray for anyone in the group who feels out of step with the world around them.
6.tip: Verses 1 to 4 can swallow the whole evening. Say once, plainly, that Christians read the "sons of God" and the Nephilim in different ways and that the text does not settle it, then move on to verses 5 to 22. Also be ready for the flood itself: Christians differ on whether it was worldwide, regional or a theological retelling, so keep the focus on what the chapter says about God's grief, human violence, Noah's trust and the promise of a covenant.

7.open: What is the worst storm or bad weather you have ever been caught in, and what did you do?
questions: God says to Noah, "I have found you righteous in this generation" (v. 1). What do you think it was like to be the one person who lived differently from everyone around him?
Verse 5 says "Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him." Noah is told to do something huge with no end in sight. When has trusting God meant doing the next step without seeing the whole picture?

Verse 11 says "all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened." Water comes from below and above at once. What picture does that give you of what was happening?
Verse 16 says "Then the LORD shut him in." Some hear that as God protecting Noah, and some hear it as a door closing on everyone else. How do you hear it, and why?

Verse 23 says "every living thing on the face of the earth was destroyed," and only Noah and those with him "remained." This is hard to read. What do you feel when you read it, and what questions does it raise about God?

Christians read this chapter differently: some as a worldwide flood, some as a large regional flood told in sweeping terms, and some as a story about judgment and rescue rather than a record of events. How can we keep learning from the chapter together even if we land in different places?

Verse 18 says "the ark floated on the surface of the waters." Noah's family was safe, but they were also shut in and carried along for months. When have you felt safe and stuck at the same time, and where was God in it for you?
7.life: This week, pick one hard or confusing part of the Bible you tend to skip. Read it slowly once, and bring your honest questions to God instead of pushing them away.
7.prayer: Thank God that he keeps and protects his people. Ask for trust to take the next step he gives, and for honesty to bring him the questions you don't know how to answer.
7.tip: Verse 23 is the hard spot. Some will want to explain it away fast and others will be troubled by it. Let the discomfort stand for a moment, say plainly that thoughtful Christians wrestle with it, and don't push the group toward one view of how big the flood was.

8.open: Think of a time you had to wait a long time for something. What helped you get through it?
questions: Verse 1 says "God remembered Noah." In the Bible, remembering usually means God turns to act, not that he had forgotten. What do you notice God doing in the first few verses?
The waters go down slowly, over months (vv. 3-5). Where in your life are you in a slow stretch right now, and how does it feel to be waiting?
Noah sends out a raven and a dove, then waits "seven more days" between tries (vv. 10, 12). What does his patience tell you about him?
Even when the ground was dry, Noah waited until God said, "Come out of the ark" (v. 16). Why might it matter to wait for God's word and not only for good signs?

The first thing Noah does after leaving the ark is build "an altar to the LORD" (v. 20). If you had just come through a hard year, what would your first move be, and what does that show about what you lean on?

God says "every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth," and still promises "Never again will I curse the ground because of man" (v. 21). How does it land with you that God makes this promise knowing people have not changed?
Verse 22 promises that "seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease." Where do you notice these steady rhythms, and how might they be a sign of God's care?
If you are honest, do you find it easy or hard to believe God is patient with you? Share as much or as little as you like.
8.life: This week, pay attention to one steady rhythm of the world, like a sunrise, a change in the weather, or something growing. Each time you notice it, thank God that he keeps his promise to sustain the earth.
8.prayer: Thank God that he remembers us and acts for us, even in long seasons of waiting. Ask him for patience in whatever you are waiting on, and for trust in his steady faithfulness.
8.tip: Verse 21 can raise the question of why God would flood the earth and then promise never to do it again. Don't try to explain it all away. Point out that the text itself says God makes this promise while knowing people's hearts are still prone to evil, and keep the group on what that shows about his patience. Many readers see the promise as resting on God's patience rather than on human improvement, but that is an interpretation, so invite different thoughts.

9.open: What is a promise someone made to you that you still remember, and why did it stick?
questions: God opens by blessing Noah and his sons and telling them to "be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth" (v. 1). Why might a fresh start after something so devastating begin with a blessing and not a warning?
God says "in His own image God has made mankind" as the reason human life matters so much (v. 6). How does that change the way you see people, including ones who are hard to like?

Verse 6 says "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man his blood will be shed." Christians disagree about whether this is a lasting rule that supports the death penalty or mainly a statement of how much every human life is worth. What do you hear in it, and why?

God says, "Never again will all life be cut off by the waters of a flood" (v. 11). Nothing is asked of Noah in return. How is a promise with no conditions different from most promises we make or receive?

The rainbow is called "a sign of the covenant" (v. 13), and God says, "I will see it and remember" (v. 16). What reminders do you use to hold on to God's promises, and what do you do on days when they feel far off?

After the flood, Noah gets drunk and lies uncovered in his tent, and Ham "told his two brothers outside" (vv. 21, 22). Why do you think Noah's story is told so honestly, right after such a high point?

Shem and Japheth cover their father with a garment, walking backward with their faces turned away (v. 23). When someone you respect fails, what does it look like to protect them and still be honest about what happened?

Noah's curse falls on Canaan (v. 25). The text does not say why, and this passage was later misused to defend enslaving Africans, though it names only Canaan. If you find this part troubling or confusing, what makes it so, and what questions would you want to ask?
9.life: The rainbow reminded Noah that God keeps his word. This week, each time you notice a reminder of God's faithfulness, such as a sunrise, a meal or a kind word, stop for ten seconds and thank him. If you find yourself doubting, say that honestly to him instead.
9.prayer: Thank God for a promise that rests on him and not on us. Ask for help to treat every person as made in his image, and to cover others' failures with care instead of gossip.
9.tip: Verses 20 to 27 are the hard spot. Say plainly that scholars are unsure exactly what Ham did and why Canaan is cursed. Make clear the curse names only Canaan and was never about Africa or skin color, and that using it to defend slavery was a serious misreading. Then return to the chapter's main thread: God's steady promise next to human weakness.

10.open: Have you ever traced your family tree or taken a DNA test? What, if anything, surprised you about where your family came from?
questions: The chapter opens with "the account of Noah's sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth" (v. 1). Why do you think the Bible includes a long list of names like this, and how do you usually react when you reach a chapter like this?

Verse 5 says the peoples spread out "according to their languages, by clans within their nations." What does it tell us that the Bible treats many languages and nations as part of the story from early on?

Nimrod is called "a mighty hunter before the LORD" (v. 9), and his kingdom grew into Babylon and Nineveh (vv. 10, 11). The text does not say whether he was admirable or proud. What do you think about power and greatness when you read his story?
Many names in this list are places and peoples Israel knew, such as Egypt, Canaan and Assyria. Why might it matter that Israel's neighbors and even rivals are placed in the same family tree?
Verse 25 says Peleg was named "because in his days the earth was divided." Scholars are unsure what that refers to. How do you handle verses where the meaning is unclear?
Verse 32 says "From these the nations of the earth spread out after the flood." Is there a group of people you find it hard to think of as distant relatives? Be as honest as you can.

Christians read this chapter differently: some as a literal family record, others as a map that uses family language for peoples. How does either reading affect what the chapter says about all people being connected?
If you came to this chapter unsure what you believe, what is one thing in it that you could accept, or one question it leaves you with?
10.life: This week, learn one thing about a person or community you usually have little contact with, such as a neighbor, coworker or someone from another culture. Listen to their story and remember that you share a common human family.
10.prayer: Thank God that every people comes from one family and that none is a stranger to him. Ask him to help you see others the way he does.
10.tip: Lists of names can feel dull, so keep the reading short and spend your time on the big picture in verse 32. If someone asks whether the list is literal, say plainly that Christians disagree, then steer back to what the chapter shows about all people being related.

11.open: What is the hardest thing you have ever tried to get a group of people to agree on, like a restaurant, a vacation or a paint color?
questions: The people said, "let us build for ourselves a city with a tower that reaches to the heavens" (v. 4). What do you think they were really after, and what do you notice about how often they say "us" and "ourselves"?
They wanted to "make a name for ourselves" (v. 4). Where do you see that same longing today, in work, family, social media or even church?
Verse 5 says "the LORD came down to see the city and the tower." What do you make of the picture of God stooping down to look at something people thought reached the heavens?
God says that as one people, "nothing they devise will be beyond them" (v. 6). When does working together bring out the best in people, and when does it start to do harm?

Christians read the ending differently. Some see pride being judged, and others see God's gift of diversity and a check on any single controlling power. What do you notice in the text that fits either view?
Verse 30 says plainly, "Sarai was barren; she had no children." Why might the writer place such a flat, quiet sentence right after the big story of Babel?
Terah set out for Canaan, but "when they arrived in Haran, they settled there" (v. 31). Have you ever started toward something and stopped halfway? What happened?
If you are honest, is it easier right now to trust God with big plans or with long waits and unanswered questions? Say as much or as little as you like.
11.life: This week, notice one moment when you are working to be seen or to build your own name. Pause, and quietly hand that moment over to God. Then do one small thing for someone that no one else will know about.
11.prayer: Thank God that he comes down to meet us rather than waiting for us to climb up. Ask him to loosen your grip on your own plans, and to help you keep going where you have stalled.
11.tip: The genealogy in verses 10 to 26 can lose the room quickly, so read it briefly or skip it, and spend your time on the Babel story and Terah's family. If someone raises whether the ages are literal or why the language of verse 7 says "Us," say that thoughtful Christians and Jewish readers differ, note it in a sentence, and return to the main question.

12.open: Have you ever moved somewhere new or started something where you didn't know anyone? What was the first week like?
questions: God tells Abram to leave "your country, your kindred, and your father's household" (v. 1). What would be hardest for you to leave, and why?
God says, "I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you" (v. 2). What do you notice about what God promises and what he asks Abram to do?

Verse 3 says "all the families of the earth will be blessed through you." Why do you think the blessing was meant to reach beyond Abram's own family? How do Christians read this line in light of Jesus?

Verse 6 says "the Canaanites were in the land" when God promised it to Abram's offspring. How might that have felt for Abram? Christians differ on how these land promises apply today, some seeing a direct link to the Jewish people and others seeing a wider fulfillment through Jesus and the church. How can we talk about that kindly?
Abram built altars and "called on the name of the LORD" along the way (v. 8). What are the simple habits or moments that help you remember God in the middle of a journey?

When famine came, Abram said to Sarai, "Please say you are my sister, so that I will be treated well for your sake" (v. 13). What was he afraid of, and who paid the price for his plan? The story never tells us what Sarai felt. What do you imagine?

Pharaoh asks, "What have you done to me?" (v. 18). It is strange that an outsider rebukes the man of faith. What do you make of that, and when has someone outside your faith shown you something you needed to see?

Abram was brave enough to leave home on a promise, yet fearful enough to put Sarai at risk. If you are honest, where do faith and fear sit side by side in your own life right now, and what do you do with the doubts?
12.life: Think of one place where fear has been steering a decision. This week, tell God about it plainly, and if someone else is affected by your choice, consider talking with them honestly.
12.prayer: Thank God that his promises do not depend on how well we do. Ask for trust to take the next step he shows you, and for honesty where fear has made us cut corners.
12.tip: Verses 11 to 20 can leave people uneasy, especially about Sarai and about why Pharaoh's household suffered. The text does not explain it, so do not force an answer. Name the discomfort, note that the Bible shows its heroes' failures openly, and point the group to the grace in the story: the promise held even when Abram did not.

13.open: Have you ever had to share a space, like a room, a car or a kitchen, with someone and found it harder than you expected?
questions: Abram returns to the place where he had built the altar, and "there Abram called on the name of the LORD" (v. 4). Why might he have wanted to go back to that exact spot? Is there a place or habit you return to when you need a fresh start?
Verse 6 says the land could not support both men because "they had so many possessions." How can having more make life harder instead of easier?

Abram says, "Please let there be no contention between you and me" and reminds Lot, "we are kinsmen" (v. 8). Why do you think he puts the relationship ahead of the land? When has a disagreement over money or things strained a relationship you cared about?
As the older man, Abram could have chosen first, but he gave Lot the choice (v. 9). What do you think that cost him, and what might it show about how he trusted God?

Lot "looked out and saw" a valley "well watered like the garden of the LORD" (v. 10). What was good about his choice, and what did he leave out of the picture? Some readers see Lot as plainly foolish here and others see him as simply doing what any herdsman would do. Where do you land?
Verse 13 says "the men of Sodom were wicked," yet Lot "pitched his tent toward Sodom" (v. 12). How do we sometimes drift toward something one small step at a time, drawn by what looks good?

After Lot leaves, God says, "Now lift up your eyes" and promises Abram the land and a family too many to count (vv. 14-16). Abram gave up the first choice and was not left empty-handed. Do you find that easy or hard to believe about God? Say honestly where you are today.
Abram answers the promise by building "an altar to the LORD" (v. 18). What is one way we can respond to God's goodness with worship, even before we see how things turn out?
13.life: Think of one relationship where you have been holding tightly to your own way, whether over money, time or plans. This week, find one small, concrete way to let the other person go first, and notice how it feels.
13.prayer: Ask God for a heart that values people over possessions, and for the trust to let go of the best seat. Pray for anyone in the group who is in a strained family relationship.
13.tip: Verses 14 to 17 raise the question of whether the land promise still applies to a literal territory today, and Christians differ on this. Say that plainly in a sentence, then steer back to the chapter's main thread, which is Abram's generosity and God's faithfulness. Also be careful not to turn Abram's choice into a formula that says giving things up always pays off, since the text simply shows God keeping his promise.

14.open: Who is someone who has come through for you when you really needed help?
questions: Four kings carry off Sodom's goods and people, and "Lot and his possessions" go with them because he "was living in Sodom" (v. 12). How does a choice made earlier, like where to live, end up shaping what happens to Lot here?

When Abram "heard that his relative had been captured," he went after him (v. 14). Lot had earlier taken the better land for himself. Why do you think Abram went anyway, and who in your life might be worth going after?
Abram brought "the 318 trained men born in his household" (v. 14). What does that detail tell you about how much Abram had grown in wealth and strength since we first met him?

Melchizedek "brought out bread and wine" and blessed Abram, saying God "has delivered your enemies into your hand" (vv. 18, 20). Why might it matter that he gives God the credit for the win, and not Abram?
Abram gave Melchizedek "a tenth of everything" (v. 20). What does giving away part of a victory say about who Abram thinks it belongs to? What does generosity look like for you right now?

Abram refuses even "a thread, or a strap of a sandal" from the king of Sodom, so no one could say "I have made Abram rich" (vv. 22-23). Where do you see the pull to take a reward that comes with strings attached?

Abram says he has "raised my hand to the LORD God Most High" (v. 22). Some people feel sure of God and some are still wrestling. What has helped you, or what would help you, trust that God is really involved in your life?
Melchizedek is a mysterious figure, and Christians understand him in different ways. What questions does this chapter raise for you, and which ones are you comfortable leaving open for now?
14.life: Think of one person who is in trouble or drifting, perhaps someone who has made choices you wouldn't. This week, reach out to them with a call, a visit or practical help, with no strings attached.
14.prayer: Thank God that he is the one who gives victory and every good thing. Ask for the courage to go after the people who need help, and for a heart that doesn't grab for more than it needs.
14.tip: The war names in verses 1 to 9 can swallow the whole meeting. Give them one minute, say that scholars can't firmly match these kings to other records, and move on to Abram's choices. On Melchizedek, say plainly that most Christians see a real king who points ahead to Jesus, while some think he was an appearance of Christ himself, and don't try to settle it.

15.open: Think of a promise someone made you, big or small. What made you believe they would keep it, or doubt that they would?
questions: God begins with "Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward" (v. 1). What do you think Abram was afraid of, and what do you tend to be afraid of these days?

Abram answers with an honest complaint: "what can You give me, since I remain childless" (v. 2). What does it say about God that Abram is allowed to speak this bluntly? Where do you find it hard to be that honest with him?
God takes Abram outside and says, "count the stars, if you are able" (v. 5). Why might God use something Abram could see, rather than just repeating the promise?

Verse 6 says, "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness." In your own words, what do you think it means to trust God, and how is that different from simply agreeing with facts about him?

Christians read verse 6 a little differently. Some stress trust alone, and others stress that real trust shows up in how a person lives. How does each view sound to you, and where do you land as you think it over?

In verse 8 Abram asks, "how can I know that I will possess it?" and God does not scold him. Instead he gives Abram a sign. When have you wanted some kind of assurance from God? What did you get, or what are you still waiting for?
In verse 17 the firepot and torch pass between the animal pieces while Abram does not. In that culture this was a way of swearing an oath. What does it tell you that God takes the promise on himself?
God tells Abram that his descendants will be "enslaved and mistreated four hundred years" before the promise is fulfilled (v. 13). How do you hold together a good promise and a long, hard wait?
15.life: Pick one thing you are still waiting on or worried about. Take it outside this week, ideally at night, look up, and tell God honestly where you are with it, doubts included. Then write down one thing he has already been faithful about.
15.prayer: Thank God that he is a shield and that he keeps his promises even when we cannot see how. Ask for honest trust, and pray for anyone in the group who is waiting on something right now.
15.tip: The list of nations and the line about the Amorites in verse 16 may raise hard questions about God giving land to one people and judging others. Don't rush to settle it. Say plainly that many readers find it troubling, let people voice that, and bring the group back to the main thread: God makes a promise and binds himself to keep it.

16.open: Think of a time you were waiting on something and got impatient. What did you do?
questions: Sarai says, "the LORD has prevented me from bearing children," and offers her maidservant to Abram (v. 2). What was Sarai trying to solve, and why might her plan have seemed reasonable to her then?
Hagar was an enslaved woman, and the text never says what she wanted. How does it change the way you read verses 1 to 4 to start from her place in the story?

When trouble comes, Sarai blames Abram, and Abram says, "Do whatever you want with her" (vv. 5, 6). Where do you see people passing the blame or stepping back from responsibility? Where do you see that in yourself?
Hagar "fled" after being treated harshly (v. 6). Have you ever wanted to run from a place or a person? What was that like?

The angel is the first to call her by name and asks, "where have you come from, and where are you going?" (v. 8). Why might God ask a question when he already knows the answer? How would you answer it right now?

The angel tells Hagar to return and submit (v. 9). Christians read this differently: some see protection for a pregnant woman in the desert, others find it deeply troubling. What do you make of it, and why should we be careful about using it as a rule for people today?
Hagar says, "You are the God who sees me" (v. 13). Has there been a time you felt unseen or unheard? If you are unsure God sees you, what would help you say that honestly?

Ishmael's name means that "the LORD has heard your cry of affliction" (v. 11). Hagar goes back to the same hard household. What difference can being truly seen and heard make when circumstances stay the same?
16.life: Notice one person this week who is easy to overlook, such as a coworker, a neighbor or someone at church. Learn their name or ask them a real question, and listen to the answer.
16.prayer: Thank God that he sees and hears people who feel overlooked. Ask him to show you where you are hurting or running, and to open your eyes to someone else who needs to be seen.
16.tip: People will want to settle whether Abram and Sarai were wrong or whether Hagar was wronged. Both are in the text, so let both be said. Be careful with verse 9: say plainly that this tells what happened to Hagar and is not an instruction for anyone today to stay with someone harming them. If someone in the room has lived through mistreatment, handle that moment gently and do not rush past it.

17.open: Have you ever been given a nickname, or changed your name, and what did it say about you?
questions: God opens with "I am God Almighty. Walk before Me and be blameless" (v. 1). What do you think it means to live openly before God with a whole heart, and how is that different from being perfect?
Abram falls "facedown" when God speaks (v. 3). What helps you take God seriously without being afraid of him?
God gives Abram a new name, Abraham, "for I have made you a father of many nations" (v. 5). Abraham was 99 and had no child with Sarah. Why might God name him for something that had not happened yet?
Verse 7 promises "an everlasting covenant" to be "your God and the God of your descendants after you." What does it mean to you that God's promise reaches beyond one person to a whole family?
God gives circumcision as "a sign of the covenant" (v. 11), a mark in the body. What signs, habits or reminders help you remember that you belong to God?
Abraham "laughed and said to himself," "Can a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?" (v. 17). What do you think was behind that laugh: doubt, joy, disbelief, or something else?

Abraham asks, "O that Ishmael might live under Your blessing!" (v. 18), and God answers, "I have heard you, and I will surely bless him" (v. 20). What does this show you about how God treats people who are not the main line of the story?
Verse 23 says Abraham obeyed "on that very day." Where do you find it hard to act on what you believe God is asking, and what makes it easier or harder to say so honestly?
17.life: Think of one promise from God that feels too big or too far off for you. Write it down, name your honest doubts next to it, and bring both to God each day this week.
17.prayer: Thank God for keeping his promises even when we laugh or doubt. Ask him to help each person trust him with what feels impossible.
17.tip: Circumcision and the question of who receives these promises today can pull the discussion into a debate about infant baptism or the land of Israel. Say once, kindly, that Christians read this differently, then steer back to what the chapter shows about God's faithfulness and Abraham's honest response.

18.open: Tell about a time someone welcomed you warmly when you showed up unexpected, or a time you were the one doing the welcoming.
questions: Abraham "ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them and bowed low to the ground" (v. 2). He does this for strangers, before he knows who they are. What does his welcome look like in everyday life today?

Abraham hurries, and has bread baked and a calf prepared (vv. 6-7). Hospitality cost him time and effort. What gets in the way of welcoming people in your own life: busyness, a messy house, nerves, something else?

Sarah "laughed to herself" at the promise (v. 12). What do you think was behind her laugh: doubt, pain, humor, or something else? Have you ever laughed at, or quietly doubted, something you hoped for?

The LORD asks, "Is anything too difficult for the LORD?" (v. 14). Where do you find that question easy to answer, and where does it feel hard to believe? Be as honest as you like, including saying you aren't sure.

Sarah was afraid and denied she had laughed, and the LORD said, "you did laugh" (v. 15). He doesn't scold her in the text. What does that moment show you about how God deals with our fear and our doubt?
The LORD asks, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" (v. 17). Why do you think God chose to share this with Abraham, and what might it say about how God treats those who follow him?

Abraham asks, "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (v. 25). When something seems unfair, is it right to push back, even against someone with far more power? What do you notice about how Abraham does it?

Abraham keeps asking and God keeps answering, down to ten (v. 32). What does this scene suggest about prayer? Christians differ on whether Abraham's pleading changed God's course or drew out a mercy God already planned. What do you make of it?
18.life: This week, welcome someone the way Abraham did: invite a neighbor, coworker or newcomer for coffee or a meal, or simply give your full attention to someone you would normally hurry past. Also bring one honest, bold request to God in prayer, the way Abraham did.
18.prayer: Thank God that he hears honest questions and even our quiet doubts. Ask for open hands to welcome others, and for the boldness to bring your real concerns to the Judge of all the earth.
18.tip: Verses 20 to 33 can stir up hard feelings about judgment, and the identity of the three visitors can pull the group into a side debate. Say plainly that Christians read the visitors differently, then steer back to what is clear: Abraham's welcome, God's patience with Sarah, and Abraham's honest, bold prayer. Chapter 19 will say more about Sodom, so there is no need to settle it tonight.

19.open: Tell about a time you were a guest in someone's home and they went out of their way for you, or a time you were the host.
questions: Lot "insisted so strongly" that the visitors come into his house, and he fed them (v. 3). Why do you think hospitality to strangers mattered so much then, and where do we see it, or miss it, today?
The men of the city, "both young and old," surrounded the house (v. 4). What does it say about a place when cruelty toward outsiders has become something everyone joins in?
Lot offers his own daughters to the mob (v. 8). The text records it without approving it. How do you think we should read a story that shows a believer failing so badly?

Christians differ on what Sodom's sin was. Some stress sexual sin, and others stress violence and cruelty to strangers and the poor. Where does this chapter itself seem to put the weight, and how can we hold our differences kindly?

When Lot "hesitated," the men took hold of his hand and led the family out "because of the LORD's compassion for them" (v. 16). What does it mean to you that rescue came even while he was dragging his feet?

Lot asked to go to a small town instead of the mountains (vv. 18-20), and Lot's wife looked back (v. 26). Have you ever found it hard to leave a place or a part of your life even after you knew it was time? What held you there?
Abraham looked down and saw only smoke (v. 28), and the narrator says God "remembered Abraham" (v. 29). What do you make of the way one person's prayers and faithfulness seem to reach Lot here?

The chapter ends in a dark place, with Lot's daughters and their choices (vv. 30-38). If this chapter leaves you unsettled, confused or even angry, what part troubles you most, and what do you want to say to God about it?
19.life: Think of one place in your life where you keep hesitating to leave something you know is harming you or others. This week, tell God honestly what is holding you there, and tell one trusted person.
19.prayer: Thank God for mercy that takes us by the hand when we hesitate. Pray for anyone you know who is stuck, afraid or hurting, and for those harmed by cruelty in our own towns.
19.tip: Verses 8 and 30 to 38 are painful, and someone may be upset or have personal history with abuse. Say plainly that the text records these acts without approving them, do not rush to explain them away, and let people pass on any question. Likewise, Christians disagree about Sodom's sin, so name that once, fairly, and return to the whole chapter.

20.open: Think of a time you worried about how a new place or new people would treat you, and they turned out better than you expected. What happened?
questions: Abraham says of Sarah, "She is my sister" (v. 2). The note behind this chapter says he did the same thing in Egypt in chapter 12. Why do you think old mistakes can come back, even for people who trust God?

God comes to Abimelech in a dream and says, "You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken" (v. 3). What does this tell us about how seriously God takes the protection of a marriage and of a vulnerable person?
God says, "I have kept you from sinning against Me" (v. 6). What do you notice about God here, working even for someone outside Abraham's family?

Abimelech asks, "What have you done to us?" (v. 9). The king speaks fairly and Abraham is the one in the wrong. How does it feel to see a believer corrected by an outsider, and what might we learn from it?
Abraham explains, "Surely there is no fear of God in this place" (v. 11). Where do we tend to assume the worst about people we don't know, and how often does that turn out to be true?

Abraham's words were technically true, since Sarah really was his half sister (v. 12), yet they were meant to mislead. Where do we see half truths in everyday life, at work, at home or online, and why are they tempting?

God keeps Sarah safe even though Abraham failed her. Where have you seen God look after someone in spite of another person's mistakes, or your own? If you honestly find that hard to believe right now, what makes it hard?

Verse 17 says "Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech." Abraham was just confronted, and still God used his prayers for the people he had wronged. What does that say about how God works with imperfect people?
20.life: This week, notice one moment when you are tempted to shade the truth to protect yourself, even with something technically accurate. Choose to say it plainly instead, and thank God that he is not waiting for you to be perfect first.
20.prayer: Thank God that he keeps his promises even when his people fail. Ask him to make you honest and to free you from assuming the worst about others.
20.tip: Some people will want to defend Abraham because Sarah was his half sister, or be shocked that God still blesses him. Gently hold both truths: the chapter does not excuse Abraham, and it does not abandon him. Keep the focus on God's faithfulness, and do not rush to a verdict on Abraham's character.

21.open: What is something you waited a long time for, and how did it feel when it finally came?
questions: Verse 1 says "the LORD did for Sarah what He had promised." Abraham and Sarah waited years, and both had once laughed in disbelief. What does it say about God that he keeps a promise people had stopped expecting?
Sarah says, "God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me" (v. 6). Tell about a time when good news in your life felt too big to keep to yourself.

Sarah sees Ishmael "mocking her son" and demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away (vv. 9-10). The Hebrew word can also mean simply playing, and scholars are unsure which is meant. What do you think was going on in that household, and what pressures might have fed it?

Verse 11 says the matter "distressed Abraham greatly because it concerned his son Ishmael." Have you ever been stuck between people you love, with no clean choice? What helped, or what would have helped?

God tells Abraham, "I will also make a nation of the slave woman's son, because he is your offspring" (v. 13). What does it tell us that God cares about Ishmael even though the promised line runs through Isaac?

Hagar says, "I cannot bear to watch the boy die!" and then weeps (v. 16). Then "God heard the voice of the boy" (v. 17). When have you felt unseen in a hard place, and where, if anywhere, did you sense God was near? It is fine to say you did not.
In verses 22 and 23, Abimelech asks Abraham for a promise of fair dealing, and Abraham settles the well dispute openly. What can we learn from how he handles conflict with an outsider?
21.life: Think of someone who stands just outside a good thing happening in your family, church or workplace, someone who may feel left out. This week, reach out to them with a call, a message or an invitation, and listen more than you talk.
21.prayer: Thank God for keeping his promises, even slow ones. Pray for anyone you know who feels sent away or overlooked, and ask God to hear them as he heard Hagar and Ishmael.
21.tip: The sending away of Hagar and Ishmael will stir strong feelings, and some may be angry at Abraham, Sarah or even God. Say plainly that Christians read this differently: some see God approving the plan, others a family failure that God permits and then answers by rescuing the outcasts. Let people be honest, then point the group to verses 17 to 19, where God hears and provides.

22.open: Who is someone you would follow without asking many questions, and what earned that trust?
questions: The first verse tells us "God tested Abraham" (v. 1), but Abraham is never told it is a test. How does knowing that change the way you read the story?
God describes Isaac as "your only son Isaac, whom you love" (v. 2). Why do you think the writer piles up so many words about how much Isaac means to Abraham?

Abraham tells his servants, "we will return to you" (v. 5). Some readers think he trusted God to spare Isaac, even to raise him. Others think he simply could not bring himself to say the truth. What do you hear in his words?

Isaac asks, "where is the lamb for the burnt offering?" and Abraham answers, "God Himself will provide the lamb" (vv. 7-8). If you were Abraham, what would you have said, and what would you have been feeling?
This story is hard to read. What stirs in you when you hear it? Is there anything here you struggle to understand, or struggle to accept about God?
The angel says, "now I know that you fear God" (v. 12). What do you think it means to fear God here, and how does that differ from being afraid of him?
Abraham names the place "The LORD Will Provide" (v. 14). Where have you seen God provide, or where are you still waiting to see it?

God promises that "through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed" (v. 18). Christians have long read this story alongside Jesus, the Father's own Son. Where do you see that connection, and what does it say about who God is?
22.life: Think of one place where you are being asked to trust God without seeing how things will turn out. Each day this week, say to him honestly where you are, whether that is trust, fear or doubt.
22.prayer: Thank God that he provides. Ask for honesty about your questions with this chapter, and for trust to take one step forward in something you cannot see the end of.
22.tip: This chapter troubles many people, and Christians read it differently: some see Abraham's obedience as a model of trust, others see a troubling command to wrestle with. Do not rush to defend God or explain the discomfort away. Let people say what disturbs them, and point out that the story ends with God stopping the sacrifice and providing.

23.open: Has there been a place, like a house, a town or a favorite spot, that felt like home to you even though it wasn't technically yours?
questions: Verse 2 says Abraham "went out to mourn and to weep for her." What stands out to you about how the Bible shows grief here, and how does your own family or culture handle it?
Abraham says, "I am a foreigner and an outsider among you" (v. 4). After decades in the land God promised him, why do you think he still describes himself this way?
The Hittites call him "God's chosen one among us" and offer "the finest of our tombs" (v. 6). What does it tell you that neighbors who did not share his faith still respected him?
Abraham bows down to the people of the land twice (vv. 7, 12). What do you notice about how he treats the people around him while he is hurting?

Ephron says, "I give you the field," then mentions "four hundred shekels of silver" (vv. 11, 15). Some readers see polite bargaining and others see real generosity. How do you read it, and why might Abraham insist on paying anyway?
Abraham was promised the whole land, yet the only piece he owns is a grave. How might it feel to wait on a promise from God and see only a small part of it in your lifetime?

Abraham chose to put down a deposit on the future right in the middle of his grief. Where are you holding on to hope for something you have not yet seen, or finding that hard to do? It is fine to answer honestly if hope feels thin right now.
Sarah was buried with care, in public, with a clear deed (vv. 17 to 20). What does that say about how God and God's people value a single life, even after death?
23.life: Think of someone who is grieving, or who is far from home, and do one small practical thing for them this week, like a meal, a call or simply sitting with them. Let them talk about the person or place they miss.
23.prayer: Thank God for the people you have loved and lost, and ask for comfort for anyone in the group who is grieving. Pray for patience to trust God's promises that are still unfinished.
23.tip: A chapter about a land purchase can feel dry, and someone may bring up modern disputes over Hebron. Gently steer back to Abraham's grief, his courtesy and his faith, and say that this study is not the place to settle present-day politics.

24.open: Tell about a time you were given a job or errand that someone else trusted you to do well. How did it go?
questions: Abraham makes his servant promise not to take a wife for Isaac from "the daughters of the Canaanites" (v. 3). What do you think Abraham was most worried about, and what do we learn about what he valued?
Abraham tells the servant that the LORD "will send His angel before you" (v. 7). Where in your life right now would it help to believe God is going ahead of you?
The servant prays, "please grant me success today, and show kindness to my master Abraham" (v. 12). What do you notice about the way he prays? How is it like or unlike the way you pray?

Rebekah gives him a drink and then says, "I will also draw water for your camels" (v. 19). Why might the servant have chosen a test that showed her character and not just her looks? What does that say about what matters in a person?
Verse 21 says the servant "watched her silently" to see whether the LORD had made his journey a success. When have you had to wait and watch before you knew whether something was right?

The servant says, "the LORD has led me on the journey" (v. 27). When you look back on your own life, where can you see something that might have been God's leading, even if you did not see it at the time? If you honestly cannot say, what makes it hard?

Laban and Bethuel say, "This is from the LORD" (v. 50), but the family also asks Rebekah, "Will you go with this man?" and she says, "I will go" (v. 58). What strikes you about her answer, and what might it have cost her?

Christians differ on whether asking God for a specific sign, as the servant did, is a pattern to follow today or just what happened in this one story. What do you think, and how do you tend to look for God's guidance?
24.life: Think of one decision you are facing. This week, pray about it each day, ask one wise person for their view, and then notice what you learn, without demanding a sign.
24.prayer: Thank God for being faithful to people who trust him, as he was to Abraham's household. Ask him to lead each person in the group in their next step, and to give patience while they wait.
24.tip: Verses 12 to 14 can lead to a debate about asking God for signs, and some people may feel guilty or confused about how they make decisions. Say plainly that Christians see this differently, then steer the group back to what the story shows: a servant who prays, waits, and gives God the credit.

25.open: What is a meal or snack you would give almost anything for when you are really hungry?
questions: Abraham's sons Isaac and Ishmael, long separated, "buried him in the cave of Machpelah" together (v. 9). What does it say about family that a funeral can bring people back to the same place?
Verse 11 says that "After Abraham's death, God blessed his son Isaac." Why might it matter that God's promise did not end when Abraham died?
Isaac "prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she was barren" and the LORD heard him (v. 21). What does it look like to pray for someone you love while you wait for an answer?

When the twins struggled inside her, Rebekah asked, "Why is this happening to me?" (v. 22). Then she went to inquire of the LORD. When life is confusing, where do you tend to take your questions first?
God tells Rebekah that "the older will serve the younger" (v. 23). That cuts against what people expected then. What does it show about how God works?
Verse 28 says Isaac loved Esau and Rebekah loved Jacob. What can happen in a home when parents have favorites, and what might it cost each person?

Esau says, "I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?" (v. 32), and the writer concludes that he "despised his birthright" (v. 34). When have you seen someone, maybe yourself, trade something lasting for something urgent?
Neither brother looks admirable in this scene. If you are honest, which one do you see more of yourself in, and why?
25.life: This week, notice one moment when something urgent pulls at you, like a craving, a deadline or an argument you want to win. Before you act, ask yourself what lasting thing you might be trading for it.
25.prayer: Thank God that he keeps his promises from one generation to the next. Ask him for patience when you are waiting, and for wisdom to value what lasts.
25.tip: Verse 23 is debated. Christians differ on whether it is mainly about God choosing individuals for salvation or about the roles of two nations in history. Say that plainly in one line, then bring the group back to what the chapter shows about Esau, Jacob and the family, and don't try to settle it tonight.

26.open: What is something you inherited from a parent or grandparent, good or bad, like a habit, a saying, or a recipe?
questions: God tells Isaac, "Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you" (v. 2). Why might staying put in a famine have felt like the harder choice?
God promises, "I will be with you and bless you" (v. 3). What does it say about God that he makes this promise before Isaac has done anything?
Isaac says Rebekah is "my sister" because "he was afraid" (v. 7). When has fear led you to say or do something you later wished you could take back?
It is Abimelech, an outsider, who sees the truth and protects the couple (vv. 8 to 11). What do you make of God's people being corrected by someone outside the faith?

Isaac grows wealthy, and the Philistines respond with envy, blocking up his father's wells (vv. 12 to 15). Why can someone else's blessing be so hard to watch? Where have you felt that, on either side?

Isaac keeps moving and digging, and he names the wells Esek, Sitnah and finally Rehoboth, saying, "At last the LORD has made room for us" (v. 22). What do those names tell you about how he handled conflict? What would it look like to answer opposition this way today?
At Beersheba God says, "Do not be afraid, for I am with you" (v. 24). If you are honest, where do you find it hard to believe that right now, and what would help?

Abimelech's men say, "We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you" (v. 28), even after sending Isaac away. What might people around you notice about how you live, and what do you hope they notice?
26.life: Isaac reopened the wells his father dug. This week, think of one good thing someone gave you, like a habit of prayer, kindness or faithfulness, and do something to keep it flowing. Thank the person if you can. If there is a harmful pattern in your family or in yourself, name it honestly to God.
26.prayer: Thank God for being with us before we have earned anything. Ask him to calm the fears that make us hide the truth, and to make room for us and for people we find hard to get along with.
26.tip: Verse 7 may spark quick judgment of Isaac, or confusion about why the story is told. Keep it gentle. Point out that Isaac repeats his father's mistake, yet God still keeps the promise. Ask the group to talk about fear and inherited habits rather than rating Isaac's character.

27.open: Did you ever pretend to be someone you weren't, even as a kid, to get something you wanted? What happened?
questions: Rebekah tells Jacob, "Your curse be on me, my son" (v. 13). Why do you think Jacob goes along with her? When have you gone along with a plan you weren't sure about because someone you trusted pushed you?

Jacob's only worry is getting caught and bringing a curse on himself (v. 12). What does that tell us about where his heart is? How easy is it to worry more about being found out than about doing wrong?

Jacob tells his father, "Because the LORD your God brought it to me" (v. 20). Why is it especially troubling to bring God into a lie? Where do we sometimes use religious words to cover something less than honest?

Isaac says, "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau" (v. 22). He senses something is off and goes ahead anyway. What does that say about how we can ignore our own doubts when we want something to be true?

When Esau finds out, he cries, "Bless me too, O my father!" (v. 34) and asks, "Haven't you saved a blessing for me?" (v. 36). What do you hear in his cry? Who in this family do you feel most sorry for, and why?

Rebekah had been told before the boys were born that the older would serve the younger, yet the family ends up broken. Christians read this differently. Some see Rebekah and Jacob as carrying out God's word by wrong means. Others see everyone at fault and God moving his purpose forward in spite of them all. If you're unsure how God works through flawed people, or whether he should, what do you honestly think?

Rebekah sends Jacob away and asks, "Why should I lose both of you in one day?" (v. 45). What did this scheme cost her and the family? Think of a time when a shortcut cost a relationship more than it gained. What did you learn?
27.life: Think of one place this week where you are tempted to stretch the truth, shade a story, or take a shortcut to get something good. Tell the truth there instead, and if you need to, go and make something right with someone.
27.prayer: Ask God for honesty in the small things as well as the big ones. Pray for anyone in the group who is carrying a broken family relationship, and ask for mercy and healing.
27.tip: People will want to decide who is the villain, and some will defend Jacob because God's plan seems to work out. Gently note that the chapter shows every member of the family acting badly and also makes room for Esau's real pain. Keep the group asking what the story shows, not who deserves the blame.

28.open: Have you ever had to sleep somewhere unfamiliar or uncomfortable, like a floor, a car or a tent? What was it like?
questions: Jacob leaves home with his brother angry at him and nothing in his hands. Why do you think God chose to meet him there, at the end of a day like that?
In verse 12 Jacob dreams of a ladder that "rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven." What do you think this picture was meant to tell him about God and about him?
God says, "I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac" (v. 13). Why might it matter to Jacob that God ties himself to his family's story? Whose faith has shaped yours?
God promises that "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring" (v. 14). What does it tell you that the promise reaches beyond Jacob himself?
Verse 15 says, "Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go." Where in your life right now would you most like to hear that spoken to you?

Jacob wakes and says, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it" (v. 16). Have you ever realized later that God was near when you did not notice? If you have not, what would help you notice?

Jacob's vow starts with "If God will be with me" (v. 20). Some readers hear a man still bargaining, others hear a first step of trust. How do you hear it, and what do you make of God answering with grace anyway?
Esau tries to win his father's approval by marrying another wife (vv. 8-9). When have you tried to fix a broken relationship with a quick gesture? What worked, and what did not?
28.life: Jacob marked the place where God met him. This week, pick one moment or place where you sensed God was near, even faintly, and write down a few lines about it. If you cannot think of one, ask God to show you where he is already at work in your ordinary days.
28.prayer: Thank God that he comes near to people who are tired, afraid or running. Ask him to help each person in the group notice his presence this week, in places that look like nowhere special.
28.tip: Jacob received this promise right after deceiving his father and brother, and some in the group may struggle with God blessing him anyway. Don't rush to excuse Jacob or to condemn him. Name it plainly: the promise is a gift, not a reward, and that is good news for anyone who feels they have not earned it.

29.open: Think of a time you waited a long time for something. What was it, and was the wait worth it?
questions: Jacob rolls the stone away from the well by himself when he sees Rachel (v. 10). Why do you think he does that, and what does it tell you about how he feels in this moment?

Jacob says, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel" (v. 18). The text says it "seemed but a few days because of his love for her" (v. 20). When has love or deep care made hard work feel light to you?
In the morning Jacob cries, "Why have you deceived me?" (v. 25). Jacob once deceived his own father. How do you read the way the story brings those two moments together?
Laban explains his trick with a local custom (v. 26). When have you seen someone use a rule or a tradition to excuse something that was really unfair?
Many readers see this as God disciplining Jacob for his earlier deceit. Others see it as the story simply showing how deception breeds more deception. How do you read it, and why?
Verse 31 says that "the LORD saw that Leah was unloved." What does it mean to you that God notices the person who feels overlooked?
Leah keeps hoping each son will win her husband's love: "Surely my husband will love me now" (v. 32). Why do we so often think that doing or achieving something will finally make someone love us?
At the end Leah says, "This time I will praise the LORD" (v. 35). What do you think changed for her? If you are in a place where praise feels hard, what is that like for you right now?
29.life: Think of someone in your life who tends to be overlooked, at church, at work or in your family. This week, notice them on purpose and do one small thing to let them know they are seen.
29.prayer: Thank God that he sees people who feel unloved and unnoticed. Ask him to help each person in the group rest in being known by him, and to make us people who notice others.
29.tip: Verses 23 to 30 involve deception, two wives and servant girls given as part of the arrangement. Do not let the group read the chapter as a model for marriage. Say plainly that the Bible reports these events honestly without approving them, then steer toward what the chapter shows about God seeing Leah.

30.open: When you were growing up, what did you and a brother, sister or friend compete over?
questions: Rachel says to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die!" (v. 1). Why did this matter so much to her, and what do you think was really underneath her words?
Jacob answers, "Am I in the place of God, who has withheld children from you?" (v. 2). What was fair and what was unkind in his reply? How do you usually respond when someone close to you is hurting?

Rachel and Leah name their sons in ways that keep score, like "I have wrestled with my sister and won" (v. 8). Where do you see comparison and scorekeeping at work in families, churches or friendships today?
Bilhah and Zilpah are given to Jacob, and the text never says what they thought. How should we read a story where some people are quietly used? What does it show about the cost of rivalry?
Leah hopes that "This time my husband will honor me" (v. 20). What are some ways people today look for love or respect from someone who is not giving it?

In verse 22 "God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb." Have you ever felt that God had forgotten you, or been slow to answer? Be as honest as you like, including if you are unsure he listens.

Jacob asks Laban for only the spotted and dark animals, and then uses peeled branches to grow his flock (vv. 32, 37). Christians read this differently: some see quiet trickery the story does not approve, others see fair provision for a man who had been treated unfairly. What do you make of it?
The chapter ends with Jacob "exceedingly prosperous" (v. 43), yet the family is full of tension. What does this say about the difference between having more and being at peace?
30.life: Notice one moment this week when you compare yourself to someone else. Instead of acting on it, say a short prayer for that person, and tell God honestly what you are longing for.
30.prayer: Thank God that he sees and remembers people who feel overlooked. Ask him to loosen the grip of comparison in your life, and pray for anyone in the group who is waiting on something they have wanted for a long time.
30.tip: The story involves painful treatment of Bilhah and Zilpah, and some readers will want to skip past it or defend it. Say plainly that the Bible reports these customs without approving them, give a moment to name the unfairness, and then return to the questions about rivalry and longing.

31.open: Have you ever left a job, a school or a place in a hurry? What was that like?
questions: Jacob noticed that Laban's "attitude toward him had changed" (v. 2), and then God said, "Go back to the land of your fathers" (v. 3). How do you tell the difference between pressure pushing you out and God leading you somewhere?
Jacob tells Rachel and Leah, "the God of my father has been with me" (v. 5). Where have you seen God's help in a hard workplace or family situation, even if it was quiet?

Rachel and Leah ask, "Do we have any portion or inheritance left in our father's house?" (v. 14). What did it cost these women to be treated this way, and what does it show about how they saw their father?

The text says Jacob "deceived Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away" (v. 20). Why do you think the writer says this so openly? Is there a time when slipping away felt easier than a hard conversation?
Laban chased Jacob, but God warned him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad" (v. 24). What does it say about God that he protects Jacob even though Jacob is far from perfect?

Rachel hides the idols and Jacob swears that whoever has them "shall not live" (v. 32). What do you make of a family where theft, secrets and rash words are all in play? Where do you see that pattern today?
Jacob says, "God has seen my affliction and the toil of my hands" (v. 42). Is there something you carry that you hope God has seen? You can answer honestly, even if it is hard to believe right now.

Laban's words, "May the LORD keep watch between you and me" (v. 49), sound like a warm blessing but work more like a warning. When people have wronged each other, can a clear boundary be wiser than full reconciliation? Why or why not?
31.life: Think of one relationship where trust is strained. This week, take one small honest step: say a hard thing kindly, set a fair boundary, or pray for that person by name each day.
31.prayer: Thank God that he sees our toil and stays with us even when we handle things badly. Ask for honesty, wisdom with difficult people, and peace where relationships are strained.
31.tip: The group may want to settle who was the villain, Jacob or Laban. The text shows both acting badly, and Christians differ on whether Jacob's claim that God gave him Laban's flocks is real faith or self-interest dressed in religious words. Name that in a sentence, then steer back to what the chapter shows about God's care for flawed people.

32.open: Think of a time you had to go back and face someone or something you had been avoiding. How did you feel on the way there?
questions: Jacob calls Esau "my master" and himself "your servant" (v. 4). Why do you think he speaks this way, and what do you remember about how things ended between them?

The messengers report that Esau is coming with "four hundred men" (v. 6). Jacob responds with "great fear and distress" (v. 7). When bad news arrives, what is your first instinct: plan, pray, panic, or hide?

In his prayer Jacob says, "I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant" (v. 10). What do you notice about how he prays, and what stands out about the order of what he says?
Jacob prays and also sends hundreds of animals ahead, hoping to "appease Esau" (v. 20). Do you see trusting God and making your own plans as working together or pulling against each other? Why?
Jacob sends his family across the stream and is "left all alone" (v. 24). When have you been alone with God, or with your own thoughts, and found it uncomfortable or hard?
Jacob says, "I will not let you go unless you bless me" (v. 26). Have you ever held on to God through doubt, anger or confusion? If not, what would honest wrestling look like for you right now?

The man says, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel" (v. 28). Why might a new name matter to someone who has spent his life known for grabbing and getting ahead? What name or label do you wish God would change for you?

Jacob leaves blessed, but "limping because of his hip" (v. 31). What might it mean that God's blessing and a lasting weakness came together? Christians read the wrestler differently, so how do you make sense of this scene?
32.life: Is there someone you have wronged or avoided? This week, take one small step toward them, such as a call, a message or an honest apology. Before you do, spend a few quiet minutes telling God exactly how you feel about it, as Jacob did.
32.prayer: Tell God honestly what you are afraid of facing. Ask for the courage to come to him as you are, and to hold on to him until you receive his blessing.
32.tip: Many people get stuck on who the wrestler was and how a physical fight with God could happen. Name in a line that Christians read it differently (an angel, God in human form, or Christ before his birth, and some see a vision), then steer back to what Jacob does: he is afraid, he prays, he clings, and he is changed. Also be gentle with anyone who feels their own struggle with God is a failure of faith. Jacob's wrestling ends in blessing.

33.open: Think of a time you ran into someone you hadn't seen in years. What was that moment like?
questions: Jacob puts Rachel and Joseph at the rear and "bowed to the ground seven times" as he approached (v. 3). What does this tell you about how he felt as he walked toward his brother?
Esau "ran to him and embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. And they both wept" (v. 4). What do you notice about how Esau greets him, compared with what Jacob feared?
The text never says what changed Esau's heart. Some readers credit God answering Jacob's prayer, and others credit Esau's own generosity. What do you make of that?
Jacob says seeing Esau's face "is like seeing the face of God" (v. 10). Have you ever seen forgiveness or kindness from another person that made God feel nearer?
Esau says, "I already have plenty, my brother," but Jacob presses him until he accepts (vv. 9-11). Why might it matter that the gift was received and not just offered?
Jacob does not go along with Esau to Seir but heads to Succoth instead (vv. 14-17). Some read this as sensible caution and others as old evasion. How do you read it, and why?

Welcome and trust are not always the same thing. When someone you wronged greets you warmly, or someone who hurt you wants to start over, what makes it hard to trust the welcome? You can answer honestly, even if the honest answer is that you are not sure.
Jacob ends the chapter by building an altar (v. 20). After a hard or emotional season, how do you tend to respond to God: with thanks, with silence, or with something else?
33.life: Think of one relationship that is strained or broken. This week, take one small step toward peace that fits the situation, such as a short note, a call, or a prayer for that person by name. Where it would not be safe or wise to reconnect, simply pray and ask God for wisdom.
33.prayer: Thank God for the times people have shown you more grace than you deserved. Ask for courage and wisdom to seek peace where it is possible, and for healing where it is still hard.
