33.tip: Some in the group may have a painful, unreconciled relationship and may feel pressure from this chapter to forgive and reunite right away. Point out that Jacob and Esau make peace but still go separate ways, and that Christians read that ending differently. Make it clear that welcome and trust can come at different speeds, and that no one has to resolve anything tonight.

34.open: When you were growing up, what was the rule in your family about standing up for a brother, sister or friend?
questions: Verse 2 says Shechem "took her and lay with her by force." Most readers understand this as rape. Dinah never speaks in the whole chapter. What do you notice about who gets heard and who does not?

Verse 3 says Shechem "loved the young girl and spoke to her tenderly," and in verse 12 he says, "Only give me the girl as my wife!" Why might the writer include these details, and do they change how you see him?
In verse 5 Jacob "remained silent" until his sons returned. What might have been going on in him, and when have you gone quiet in the face of something painful?
The sons were "filled with grief and fury" (v. 7). Their anger over what happened to Dinah makes sense. At what point does it turn into something else in this chapter?
Verse 13 says the brothers answered "deceitfully," using circumcision, a sign of God's promise, as part of their plan. What does it say about us when we use religious things for our own purposes?
Simeon and Levi killed every male in the city, and the other sons took the women and children. How did one man's act end up costing a whole town, and where do we see that pattern today?

Jacob says, "You have brought trouble upon me" (v. 30), and he speaks about safety, not about the killings. The brothers answer, "Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?" (v. 31). Which response do you find yourself more drawn to, and why?
God is never mentioned in this chapter. If you feel that God is silent in some part of your own life, or in a story like this one, what do you want to say about that honestly?
34.life: Think of someone who has been wronged, in your life or in the news. This week, do one thing for them that is real help, like listening, writing a note or giving your time, and bring the anger you feel on their behalf to God instead of acting on it.
34.prayer: Ask God to be close to anyone who has been hurt or silenced, and to protect them. Ask for a hunger for justice that does not turn into revenge.
34.tip: This chapter may bring up personal experiences of sexual violence in your group. Name that at the start, tell people they can pass on any question, and do not push anyone to share. Also avoid quick answers about who was right: Christians and Jews differ on how far the story condemns the brothers, so let people hold the sorrow of the chapter without forcing a tidy lesson.

35.open: Is there a place you go back to, like a childhood home or a favorite spot, that reminds you of an important time in your life?
questions: God tells Jacob to go back to Bethel, where he met God when he was running from Esau (v. 1). Why do you think God called him back to that place now?
Jacob tells his household, "Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you" (v. 2). What might it look like today for a family or a person to clear out the things that compete with God?

Jacob describes God as the one "who answered me in my day of distress" and who "has been with me wherever I have gone" (v. 3). When have you looked back and seen God's help more clearly than you did at the time?

God says, "Your name will be Israel" (v. 10). Names mattered a great deal then. What would it mean for Jacob to be given a new name by God, and what do you think it meant for him to hear it again here?
God says, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply" (v. 11). Jacob has been through years of conflict and loss. Why might it matter that God repeats the promise now?
Rachel names her baby Ben-oni, and Jacob renames him Benjamin (v. 18). What do you notice about two people responding differently to the same moment of grief?

The chapter holds worship, a birth, a death, a family betrayal and a funeral, all close together (vv. 7-29). How does this match real life, and what do you do when good and hard things arrive at the same time?
If you are in a season where God feels distant or you are not sure what you believe, what would you honestly say about where you are tonight?
35.life: Jacob went back to a place where God had met him and made it a marker. This week, take ten minutes to write down one time you saw God's help in your life. Keep it somewhere you will find it again, and thank God for it.
35.prayer: Thank God that he is faithful to his promises, even when we wander. Ask him to show us any "foreign gods" we are holding onto, and pray for anyone in the group who is grieving.
35.tip: The chapter moves quickly from worship to Rachel's death to Reuben's act to Isaac's death, so people may get stuck on the dark parts, especially verse 22, which is short and unexplained. Name it plainly, say Genesis does not comment on it here, and bring the group back to the bigger picture of God staying faithful to a flawed family.

36.open: Is there a family story that gets told at every holiday, and who always tells it?
questions: The chapter opens, "This is the account of Esau (that is, Edom)" (v. 1). Esau has mostly been a side character in Genesis. Why might the writer stop and give him a whole chapter?

Esau moved "to a land far away from his brother Jacob" because their possessions were "too great for them to dwell together" (vv. 6, 7). Have you seen distance be the healthiest choice for two people? When did it feel more like a loss?
Esau settles in Mount Seir and his family grows into a nation (v. 8). What does it say about God that Esau, who is not the chosen line, still gets a home and a future?

Christians read this chapter differently. Some see it as proof that Esau was still blessed and given a land of his own. Others see it mainly as the closing of his story so the narrative can follow Jacob. What do you notice in the text that makes sense of either view?
The list of kings says again and again that someone "reigned in his place" (vv. 33 to 39). What does that repeated phrase suggest about power and how long it lasts?

Verse 31 mentions the time "before any king reigned over the Israelites." Many scholars think this means the list was written or updated later. How does it change your view of the Bible to know it was handed down and shaped over time?
Be honest: what goes through your mind when you reach a chapter that is mostly names? Bored, puzzled, curious, something else? What would help a chapter like this mean more to you?
36.life: Think of one person you have drifted from, whether through a quarrel or just distance. This week, send a short, kind message with no agenda, or pray for them by name each day.
36.prayer: Thank God that he keeps track of every family and every name, including those outside the main story. Ask for peace with anyone you have parted from, and for trust that your own story matters to him.
36.tip: Do not read every name aloud. Read verses 1 to 8 and 31 to 43, and summarize the middle in a sentence. If someone says the chapter is boring, agree warmly and then turn to the questions about Esau's move and the kings.

37.open: Did you grow up with a family rule, a tradition or a nickname that only your family would understand? What was it?
questions: Verse 3 says Israel "loved Joseph more than his other sons" and made him a special robe. What do you think favoritism does to a family, both to the favorite and to everyone else?
In verse 4 the brothers "hated him and could not speak a kind word to him." Where have you seen resentment grow slowly until it could not be hidden?

Joseph tells his brothers about both dreams, and they "hated him even more" (v. 8). Christians read Joseph differently here: some see a blameless young man, others a tactless teenager. How do you read him, and does it change how you feel about the brothers?

When the brothers see Joseph coming, they say, "Here comes that dreamer!" and plan to kill him (vv. 19, 20). How does a person slide from bitterness to something that dark? What might have stopped them?

Reuben tries to rescue Joseph (vv. 21, 22) and Judah argues for selling him instead of killing him (vv. 26, 27). Neither fully does the right thing. What do you make of people who do a little good but not enough?

The brothers dip the robe in blood and let their father believe Joseph is dead (vv. 31 to 33). Jacob "refused to be comforted" (v. 35). Have you ever watched someone carry grief that others could not ease? What helped, or what didn't?

Nothing in this chapter mentions God stepping in, and Joseph ends it as a slave in Egypt (v. 36). If you were honest, what would you say to God, or about God, if you were in Joseph's place? Doubts and frustration are welcome here.
What does this chapter ask of us when we notice resentment toward someone in our own family, church or friend group?
37.life: Think of one person you have been cold toward, perhaps because of jealousy or an old hurt. This week, do one small kind thing for them, such as a greeting, a message or a word of real encouragement. If it is a harder situation than that, bring it honestly to God.
37.prayer: Ask God to show you any bitterness you are holding, and to heal what has been broken in your family or friendships. Pray for anyone in the group who feels overlooked, betrayed or stuck in a hard place.
37.tip: People will want to jump ahead and say that God used it for good. That comes later in the story, and it can sound hollow to someone hurting now. Let the group stay with the betrayal and the grief in this chapter first, and give people room to be honest that it feels unresolved.

38.open: Have you ever been mistaken for someone else? What happened?
questions: Judah tells Tamar, "Live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up" (v. 11), but he never follows through. What do you think is behind his choice, and what does it cost Tamar?
In that world a widow with no son had almost no protection or future. How does knowing that change the way you read what Tamar does?

Twice the text says the LORD put a son of Judah to death for being "wicked in the sight of the LORD" (vv. 7, 10). That is hard to read. What do you honestly think or feel when you come to lines like these?

When Judah thinks he might be laughed at, he says, "Let her keep the items" (v. 23). A few verses later he says, "Let her be burned to death!" (v. 24). What do you notice about what he cares about most?
Tamar does not accuse Judah in public. She simply says, "Please examine them" (v. 25). Why might she go about it this way, and what does it give Judah the chance to do?
Judah says, "She is more righteous than I" (v. 26). When was the last time you admitted you were wrong to someone? What makes that so hard?
Christians disagree about how to judge Tamar. Some see her trick as justified, and others see wrong on both sides, with her less to blame. Where do you land, and what makes it hard to decide?

Perez, the child who was named when the midwife said, "You have broken out first!" (v. 29), becomes an ancestor of King David, and Matthew names Tamar in Jesus' family line. What does it say to you that God's story runs through a family this messy?
38.life: Think of one person you have made a promise to or owe something to, such as an apology, some help or your time. Do something this week to make it right, even if it is small.
38.prayer: Thank God that he works through broken families and flawed people, and that includes us. Ask for the humility to admit when we are wrong and the courage to make it right.
38.tip: The chapter includes Onan, prostitution and a death sentence, so state the facts plainly and calmly and keep moving. On Onan, most readers focus on his refusal to give his brother an heir (v. 9), though some traditions read it differently. Say so briefly, then steer the group back to Judah and Tamar.

39.open: Tell about a time you were trusted with something important, like keys, a secret, or a big job. How did it feel?
questions: Twice we are told "the LORD was with Joseph" (vv. 2, 21). The chapter also says he was sold, accused and jailed. What do you make of both being true at once?
Potiphar "entrusted him with everything he owned" (v. 4). What does it look like to be someone others can trust, and what might it cost?
When Joseph refuses, he first points to his master's trust and then asks, "how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?" (v. 9). Why do you think he gives both reasons?
The text says she spoke to him "day after day," and he refused "or even be near her" (v. 10). What does that say about how temptation often works, and about how we can handle it?
In verse 14 she stresses that he is "this Hebrew," a foreigner with no one to defend him. Why is it so painful when someone with less power is blamed? Where do you see that happen today?

This is the second time Joseph's clothing is used to tell a lie about him. If you were Joseph sitting in that prison, what might you be feeling toward God? Say it as honestly as you can, even if the answer is doubt or anger.
Verse 21 says that in prison the LORD "extended kindness to him." Where have you seen kindness show up in a hard place, from God or from other people?
Christians differ on whether this chapter is mainly an example of resisting temptation or mainly a story of God quietly working through unfair events. Which part speaks to you tonight, and why?
39.life: Think of one place where you are tempted to cut a corner or cross a line, or one person who trusts you. This week, take one small, practical step to guard that trust, such as changing a habit or telling a friend you can count on.
39.prayer: Thank God that he is with us in good seasons and in unfair ones. Ask for honesty about what feels unjust right now, and for strength to stay faithful in small, hidden places.
39.tip: Some will want to treat this only as a lesson in resisting temptation, and others may be uneasy because Joseph is punished for doing right. Don't tidy it up. Let people say that it feels unfair, then point to the repeated line that the LORD was with him, without promising that doing right will always be rewarded quickly.

40.open: Have you ever had a dream so strange or vivid that you told someone about it the next morning? What was it?
questions: Joseph is in prison for something he did not do, yet he notices that the two officials look upset: "Why are your faces so downcast today?" (v. 7). What does it say about Joseph that he is looking out for others? How easy is that when you are hurting yourself?

When the men say no one can explain their dreams, Joseph answers, "Don't interpretations belong to God?" (v. 8). Why do you think he says this before he says anything else? What is he pointing them toward?
Joseph asks the cupbearer, "please remember me and show me kindness" (v. 14). What do you make of Joseph asking for help? When is it hard for you to ask for something you need?
Joseph tells the baker bad news, and the baker's dream ends with him hanged (vv. 19, 22). How do you think Joseph felt giving that answer? When have you had to tell someone something hard but true?
Everything happens just as Joseph said (vv. 20 to 22). What do you think that showed the two men, and Joseph himself, about who was behind the dreams?

The chapter ends with this: "The chief cupbearer, however, did not remember Joseph; he forgot all about him" (v. 23). Why do you think the writer ends on such a flat, disappointing line? What does it feel like to be forgotten after you helped someone?

The text never says why Joseph stays in prison, or what God is doing in the waiting. If you are in a waiting season right now, or have been in one, how would you honestly describe where God seems to be? It is fine to say you are not sure.
40.life: Think of one person who has helped you and may never have been thanked. This week, send them a note or message to say thank you. Then do one small, quiet kindness for someone who cannot repay it.
40.prayer: Thank God that he sees people who feel forgotten. Ask for honesty about any season of waiting you are in, and for a heart that keeps noticing others even when it is not returned.
40.tip: Some will want to explain why God let Joseph sit two more years, and others will feel the ending is unfair. Let both be said. The chapter itself gives no reason, so keep the group on what the text shows: Joseph stays faithful and the cupbearer forgets.

41.open: Have you ever had a dream, or a worry, that stuck with you all day? What was it?
questions: Pharaoh's dreams trouble him, and none of his wise men can explain them (v. 8). When something troubles us today, where do people usually go for answers?
The cupbearer finally says, "Today I recall my failures" (v. 9), two years after Joseph asked for his help. What do you think those two years were like for Joseph?

Joseph is brought "quickly" out of the dungeon (v. 14), and he answers Pharaoh, "God will give Pharaoh a sound answer" (v. 16). Why does it matter that Joseph does not take the credit? When is it hard to give credit away?
After explaining the dreams, Joseph goes on to give a plan: collect a fifth of the harvest and store it (vv. 34 and 35). What does that show about how trusting God and planning ahead can go together?
Pharaoh asks, "Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?" (v. 38). What might Pharaoh have noticed in Joseph? What do people notice in you?

Joseph names his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, saying "God has made me forget all my hardship" (v. 51) and "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction" (v. 52). Can a person feel grateful and still carry old pain? Where have you seen both at once?
The text does not say Joseph felt God's presence during the two years of waiting. If you have ever felt forgotten, or unsure that God was paying attention, what would you honestly say about that?

When the famine comes, Pharaoh tells his people, "Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you" (v. 55), and every nation comes for grain (v. 57). Who has been a source of help or comfort to you, and how could we be that for someone else?
41.life: Think of one person who may feel forgotten, like Joseph in the dungeon. This week, reach out with a call, a note or an invitation, and tell them they have been on your mind.
41.prayer: Thank God that he is not limited by our waiting or by other people's forgetfulness. Ask for patience in the places where help has not come yet, and for a willingness to give God the credit when things go well.
41.tip: Joseph's story can sound like a promise that if you wait faithfully, you will end up in a palace. Many people in the room have waited a long time with no rescue in sight. Say plainly that this chapter shows one moment in a longer story, not a formula, and make room for people to say that waiting is hard.

42.open: When you were growing up, who was the person you could never say no to, and why?
questions: Jacob asks his sons, "Why are you staring at one another?" (v. 1). When have you seen a family or a group freeze up instead of facing a problem?
Verse 6 says the brothers "bowed down before him with their faces to the ground." Why do you think the writer wants us to notice this, and what does it recall from the story so far?
Verse 8 says, "Although Joseph recognized his brothers, they did not recognize him." What do you think it was like for Joseph to stand there knowing who they were?
Joseph accuses them of being spies and jails them for three days. The story never says exactly why. What reasons might he have had, and what do you make of his behavior?

In verse 21 the brothers say, "Surely we are being punished because of our brother." Why do you think it took twenty years and a crisis for this to come out? Why do old wrongs so often come back at hard moments?
Verse 24 says Joseph "turned away from them and wept." What might those tears tell us about what he was feeling beneath the harsh words?

When the brothers find their silver in the sacks, they ask, "What is this that God has done to us?" (v. 28). When things go wrong, how do you tend to read God's hand in it? If you are unsure what God is doing in your life right now, you can say so.

Jacob says, "Everything is going against me!" (v. 36). We the readers know more of the story than he does. How does that change the way you hear his words, and what might that say about seasons in our own lives that feel that way?
42.life: Think of one old wrong, either something done to you or something you did, that you have never really faced. This week, take it to God honestly. If it involves another person, ask God whether there is a small, safe step you could take toward honesty with them.
42.prayer: Thank God that he is at work even when we cannot see it. Ask for honesty to face what we have avoided, and for trust when life feels like it is all going against us.
42.tip: Joseph's harsh treatment of his brothers can stir strong opinions. Some see a wise test, others see his own hurt at work. Say plainly that Christians read it both ways, and steer the group back to what the brothers' guilt and Jacob's fear show us.

43.open: When was the last time you were invited to a meal and had no idea what to expect?
questions: Jacob says, "Why did you bring this trouble upon me?" (v. 6). When things get hard, what is your first instinct: blame someone, hide, or fix it? Why?
Judah says, "I will guarantee his safety" and offers to "bear the guilt" all his life (v. 9). What is Judah risking here, and why might this be a big moment for him?
Jacob finally gives in and says, "As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved" (v. 14). What do you hear in those words? Have you ever had to let go of something you could not control?
Jacob prays, "May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man" (v. 14). What does it say about Jacob that he prays this even while afraid and unsure?
The brothers are "frightened" when they are taken to Joseph's house (v. 18). Why do guilt and fear so often assume the worst when kindness is being offered?

The steward says, "Do not be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure that was in your sacks" (v. 23). Where might God have been quietly at work in your life in ways you did not notice at the time?
Joseph "hurried out because he was moved to tears" and wept in private (v. 30). Why do you think he hid his feelings? When is it hard for you to let others see what you really feel?

Benjamin's portion was "five times larger than any of the others" (v. 34). Many readers see this as a quiet test of whether the brothers would resent a favored brother. How do you handle it when someone else is favored over you?
43.life: Think of one person you have struggled to trust, or one person you owe an honest apology. This week, take one small step: pray for them by name, or reach out with a kind word or an honest one.
43.prayer: Thank God that he is at work even when we cannot see it. Ask him for courage to let go of what we cannot control, and for hearts that can trust and be trusted.
43.tip: Joseph's side of the story is hidden from the brothers, so some people may feel uneasy that he is testing them rather than simply telling them who he is. Let that tension stand. Point out that the chapter shows both Joseph's tears and his caution, and invite the group to notice what each tells us about how hard it is to rebuild trust.

44.open: Think of a time someone gave you a second chance. What did that mean to you?
questions: Joseph has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack (v. 2). What do you think he was hoping to find out about his brothers, and why would he need to know?
When the cup is found, the brothers "tore their clothes" and all go back to the city together (v. 13). Why does it matter that none of them walked away?
Joseph offers the others a way out: "The rest of you may return to your father in peace" (v. 17). Why would that offer be tempting, and what would it have cost them?

Judah says, "God has exposed the iniquity of your servants" (v. 16). Many readers think he is thinking of what they did to Joseph long ago. Have you ever felt old guilt come back to the surface? What was that like?
Judah says their father's "life is wrapped up in the boy's life" (v. 30). What does this speech tell you about how Judah now sees his father and his brother?

In verse 33 Judah says, "please let your servant stay here as my lord's slave in place of the boy." This is the same Judah who once helped sell Joseph. What do you think it takes for a person to genuinely change?
Christians have often seen Judah's offer as a small picture of Jesus, who came from Judah's family line and took our place. Where do you see that connection, and where does it feel like a stretch?

Readers differ on whether Joseph's test was wise and loving, or whether it also carried some of his own hurt. How does that sit with you, and is there anything in this story you find hard to make sense of?
44.life: Think of one relationship where something old is still unresolved. This week, take one small step toward it, such as a message, a prayer for that person, or an honest apology you owe.
44.prayer: Thank God that people can change and that he is patient with us while we do. Ask him to show you where you need to grow, and to give you the kind of love that puts others first.
44.tip: Joseph's trick can feel cruel, and some in the group may be bothered by it. Let them say so. Name that Christians read his motives differently, then bring the group back to Judah's change, which is the heart of the chapter.

45.open: Tell about a time you were reunited with someone after a long time apart. What was that moment like?
questions: Joseph "could no longer control himself" and wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard (vv. 1-2). Why do you think a man with so much power let himself break down in front of the very people who hurt him?
Joseph says, "I am Joseph, your brother," and adds, "the one you sold into Egypt!" (v. 4). Why do you think he names what they did instead of skipping past it?
The brothers were "unable to answer him, because they were terrified" (v. 3). Have you ever faced someone you wronged, or someone who wronged you? What was going on inside you?

Joseph says, "do not be distressed or angry with yourselves," because "it was to save lives that God sent me before you" (v. 5). What do you hear in those words, and how might they have sounded to the brothers?

Christians read verses 5 to 8 in different ways. Some think God planned even the wrong itself, and others think God allowed a human choice and then brought good out of it. Which way of seeing it helps you, or does neither fit well right now?
Joseph embraces Benjamin first, and only after the kisses and tears "his brothers talked with him" (vv. 14-15). Why might forgiveness have to come before honest conversation can start?
As they leave, Joseph says, "Do not quarrel on the way!" (v. 24). What kinds of old arguments can follow a family even after a big moment of peace?

Jacob was stunned and "did not believe them," until he saw the wagons (vv. 26-27). When has good news felt too good to trust, and what helped you begin to believe it? It's fine to say you're still not sure.
45.life: Think of one person you are holding something against, or one you owe an apology. This week take one small step: pray for them by name, write a note, or make the call.
45.prayer: Thank God for working in the hard chapters of our lives. Ask for honesty about old hurts and for the courage to forgive or to ask forgiveness.
45.tip: Verses 5 to 8 can sound like the brothers' cruelty was fine because it turned out well, and that can sting someone who has been badly hurt. Point out that Joseph still says "you sold into Egypt" (v. 4). Seeing good come from a wrong is not the same as calling the wrong acceptable. Let people answer the disagreement question without pushing them to choose.

46.open: Think of a time you moved, changed jobs or started something new. What was the one thing you were most nervous about?
questions: Before leaving Canaan, Jacob stops at Beersheba and "offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac" (v. 1). Why might he pause to worship before a big move? What do you do before a big change?

God says, "Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt" (v. 3). Jacob was heading toward the son he had longed to see, and he still needed to hear this. Why might fear show up even when the change is a good one?
God promises, "I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back" (v. 4). What does it say about God that he promises to go along and not only to send Jacob off with a blessing?
Verses 8 to 27 are mostly names. Why might the writer take the time to list every one of them? What does it tell you about how God sees families and people?

Jacob says, "Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!" (v. 30). Have you ever waited a long time for something or someone? What was it like when the waiting ended, or what is it like if it has not ended yet?

Joseph tells his family to say plainly that they raise livestock, so they can settle in Goshen (vv. 33-34). What do you make of that plan? When have you had to be honest about who you are, even when it might not be admired?
Some of us carry a fear of what is ahead, or a doubt that God goes with us at all. If you are willing, what is one place in your life where you would like to hear God say, "Do not be afraid"?
46.life: Think of one change or worry you are facing right now. Each day this week, say God's words from verse 3 to him as a prayer: "Do not be afraid." Then tell one person in the group how it is going next time you meet.
46.prayer: Thank God that he goes with us into unfamiliar places. Ask him to calm the fears the group is carrying into what is coming next, and to bring comfort to anyone still waiting for a reunion or an answer.
46.tip: The list of names in verses 8 to 27 can make a group glaze over. Don't read it all aloud. Read verses 1 to 7 and 26 to 34, mention in one line that the middle is a family roll, and spend your time on God's promise and the reunion. If someone asks about the number seventy, say simply that the count includes Jacob, Joseph and his two sons, and that some scholars also see seventy as a round number for a complete family.

47.open: Have you ever moved to a new place or joined a new group where you didn't know anyone? What helped you settle in?
questions: The brothers tell Pharaoh plainly, "Your servants are shepherds" (v. 3). Why might it matter that they were honest about who they were, and where is it hard for you to be that plain about yourself?
Jacob answers Pharaoh, "My years have been few and hard" (v. 9). What do you make of an old man describing his life so honestly, and how does that sit next to the idea that God was with him?
Jacob blesses Pharaoh, the most powerful man in Egypt, twice (vv. 7, 10). What does that tell us about who holds real authority in this scene?
The Egyptians say, "Why should we die before your eyes?" (v. 15), and give up their money, their livestock and finally their land. What does desperation do to the choices people make?

The people say, "You have saved our lives" (v. 25), yet they have become Pharaoh's servants. Christians read Joseph's actions differently here, some as wise rescue and some as a troubling use of power. What do you see, and what makes it hard to decide?
Verse 27 says the Israelites "became fruitful and increased greatly in number." What do you notice about the gap between their situation and the Egyptians' situation in the same chapter?
Jacob asks, "Do not bury me in Egypt" (v. 29), even after seventeen good years there. Where do you feel pulled between a comfortable place and a deeper sense of home or promise?
If you are not sure what to make of a God who seems to work through messy and uneven circumstances like these, what questions would you honestly want to ask?
47.life: Think of one person who is struggling right now, whether with money, work or a hard season. This week, do one specific thing to help them without taking anything from them: a meal, a ride, a call or some of your time.
47.prayer: Thank God that he keeps his promises even when life looks uncertain and unfair. Ask for honesty about your own hard years, and for a heart that uses whatever influence you have to help people rather than take from them.
47.tip: The land purchase in verses 13 to 26 will split the group. Some will praise Joseph and some will find it troubling. Say once that Christians read it both ways, ask people to point to the words in the text, and don't push for a verdict. Also note that verse 21 is translated differently in different Bibles, so don't let a side comment about wording derail the discussion.

48.open: Who is someone older than you who has spoken a good word over your life, and what did they say?
questions: Jacob is old, ill and nearly blind, yet he "rallied his strength and sat up in bed" to receive Joseph and the boys (v. 2). What does that tell you about how much this blessing mattered to him?
Jacob says, "I never expected to see your face again," and now he has seen Joseph's children too (v. 11). Where have you been given something you never expected to receive?
Joseph says his sons are "the sons God has given me in this place" (v. 9). Joseph's boys were born in Egypt, far from home. How can you see God's gifts in a place that doesn't feel like home?
Jacob speaks of "the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day" (v. 15). Looking at your own life, what has God's care looked like, including the times it was hard to see?
Jacob crosses his hands and puts the greater blessing on the younger boy, even though Manasseh was the firstborn (v. 14). Why do you think Joseph found this so upsetting (vv. 17, 18)?
Jacob answers Joseph, "I know, my son, I know!" (v. 19). He had been the younger son himself and received a blessing he did not earn. What does this chapter suggest about how God hands out blessing?
Jewish parents still use the words "May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh" (v. 20). If you were to bless a child or friend in your own words, what would you ask God to give them?
48.life: This week, speak a blessing out loud over someone younger than you, a child, a student or a friend. Keep it short and honest, and ask God to be their shepherd the way he was Jacob's.
48.prayer: Thank God for the people who have prayed for you and spoken good over you. Ask him to help each person in the group to bless others, and to trust his care in places that feel unfamiliar.
48.tip: Some will feel the sting of the younger son being chosen over the older, and Joseph's objection gives them room to say so. Let them. Then point back to verse 19, where Jacob is not praising one boy over the other. Both are blessed, and God is the one choosing. Verse 16 mentions an angel, and many Christians read this as Christ while others do not, so say that gently and move on. Verse 22 is unclear to scholars, so do not spend time on it.

49.open: What is something your family always says or does that people outside the family might find odd?
questions: Jacob says he will tell his sons "what will happen to you in the days to come" (v. 1). If someone who knew you well described you in a few lines, what do you hope they would say, and what would you dread?
Reuben was the firstborn, "excelling in honor, excelling in power," yet Jacob says he "will no longer excel" (vv. 3-4). How can a person's past choices shape what they become, even years later?

Of Simeon and Levi, Jacob says, "Cursed be their anger, for it is strong" (v. 7). He condemns the anger, not the sons themselves. Why might that difference matter, and where do you see anger shaping a family?
Judah is called "a young lion" and is given the leading place among his brothers (vv. 8-9). Judah's own story was far from spotless. What does it say about God that he chooses someone like this?

Verse 10 speaks of the scepter and "Shiloh." Christians read it differently, some as a direct promise of Jesus and others as first about David's line and later seen in Jesus. How do you hear it, and what do you find hard about a verse like this?

Joseph was attacked by archers "with bitterness," yet "he steadied his bow" by the hands of "the Mighty One of Jacob" (vv. 23-24). When have you felt God steadying you through something that was aimed at you?
Jacob asks to be buried with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah and Leah in Canaan (vv. 29-31). What does that wish show about where he placed his hope? Where do you want your own hope to rest?

Verse 28 says Jacob "blessed each one with a suitable blessing," even though some of the words were hard. If you are honest, which son's words do you find most comforting, and which most unsettling? Why?
49.life: Think of one person in your family or close circle. This week, tell them one specific strength you see in them, and if there is an old hurt between you, pray about one small step toward peace.
49.prayer: Thank God that he knows each of us fully and still stays with us. Ask for honesty about our own failures, and for the grace to speak words that build up the people we love.
49.tip: Verses 3 to 7 can leave people uneasy, since the words about Reuben, Simeon and Levi are hard. Say plainly that Jacob is naming real wrongs, and point the group toward Judah and Joseph, where God's grace shows up in flawed people. Don't rush to tidy up the hard sayings, and keep the verse 10 disagreement brief and friendly.

50.open: Think of a time a family gathering, like a funeral, wedding or reunion, brought up something that had been quietly sitting under the surface. What was that like?
questions: Joseph "fell upon his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him" (v. 1). What does this tell you about Joseph, and how do you think people in our culture handle grief compared to this?
Joseph's brothers think, "What if Joseph bears a grudge?" (v. 15). Even after years of kindness, they still fear him. Why might guilt linger long after someone has been treated well?

The brothers pass along a message said to be from their father (vv. 16-17), though the text never says Jacob gave it. Some readers think they may have made it up. How does the way they approach Joseph show what they believed about him?

When the brothers bow down and say, "We are your slaves!" (v. 18), Joseph weeps (v. 17) and tells them, "Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?" (v. 19). What do you think he means, and why might that question be hard to live by when we have been hurt?
Joseph says, "what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good" (v. 20). He does not say the evil was not evil. How is that different from saying the harm was secretly fine?

Christians read verse 20 differently. Some see God as planning even the wrong, others see God bringing good out of a wrong he did not cause. Where do you find yourself leaning, and what questions does it leave you with?

Joseph "reassured his brothers and spoke kindly to them" (v. 21). What does forgiveness look like in practice when someone is still afraid of you? Is there anyone you struggle to reassure, or to be reassured by?

Joseph's last words are, "God will surely visit you" (v. 24), though his coffin is still in Egypt when the book ends (v. 26). If you are waiting on something from God and see no sign of it yet, what is that like for you? Honest answers, including doubt, are welcome here.
50.life: Think of one person you have wronged or one who has wronged you. This week, take one small step toward them, such as a kind message, a prayer for them by name, or an honest word to a friend about how you are struggling to forgive.
50.prayer: Thank God that he is able to bring good out of painful things without calling the pain good. Ask him for the grace to forgive, to receive forgiveness, and to trust him in the long waits.
50.tip: Verse 20 can sound like a quick answer to someone who has been badly hurt. Make clear that Joseph does not tell his brothers what they did was fine, and that nobody has to feel grateful for harm done to them. Name the disagreement about God and evil once, kindly, and move on without trying to settle it.
